av_event.what: Abena laughs silently with her mouth closed, her shoulders shaking for a couple of seconds, and briefly looks down and away from the camera before looking back

text:
A: Hello. Karen, is it?
B: Yeah. Hi.
A: I'm Abena. I'm in South London, Herne Hill. Where are you?
B: Taunton. Somerset.
A: Oh, lovely. I don't know it well. We drove through once on the way to Cornwall, I think.
B: Most people do. Drive through.
A: Well. What do you do there?
B: I manage a charity shop. Hospice shop, on the high street.
A: Oh, really? I spend a lot of time in charity shops. Well, more the vintage and antique places, but charity shops too, if they have furniture.
B: We don't do much furniture, not enough room. Bit of small stuff. Lamps, mirrors. Mostly clothes and books.
A: That's still interesting. I'm an interior designer, part-time, so I'm always looking. There's a mid-century sideboard in a shop in Crystal Palace I keep going back to look at. Teak. I'm sort of in love with it.
B: Go on then, how much?
A: Erm. Too much, probably. Nine hundred.
B: Nine hundred. For a sideboard. We had one in last year, looked just like that, I priced it at sixty and it went in half an hour.
A: Then I've been shopping in the wrong place. Do you price everything yourself?
B: Most of it. You get quick. And you learn the labels. Someone'll bring in a bag of jumpers and there's a cashmere one at the bottom they've no idea about.
A: That's a real skill. Knowing what something is worth at a glance. I do something similar with clients, I suppose. They say they want one thing, and you have to hear what they actually want.
B: Yeah, I suppose. People don't always say what they mean. Volunteers neither.
A: Oh?
B: Saturdays. They'll say, yeah, I'll be in, and then half eight, text. Every week. I end up doing the till and the back room on my own.
A: That sounds exhausting.
B: It is. Then I'm short with them on the Monday and I lie awake about it. Sorry, was that what you meant? You only said "oh".
A: No, no, it was. Please, go on. I was just listening.
B: That's it really. What else do you do, apart from the designing?
A: Well. Galleries, mostly. I walk in Brockwell Park in the mornings. And church, on Sundays. It's harvest coming up and I've been roped into the decorations, so it's flowers and marrows this weekend.
B: Which church?
A: A Ghanaian Methodist congregation. I'm from Accra originally.
B: Oh, I'm Methodist. Well, I go to the chapel here. Twice a month, maybe. More at Christmas.
A: Really? Then you'll know harvest. Somebody always brings a tin of something nobody can identify.
B: Every year. Ours had a tin of mushy peas from about 1990 last time. Same as the shop. People clear their cupboards out and call it giving.
A: Erm, I'll be honest, for me it's mostly the people and the singing. I'm not sure how devout I am.
B: Same, sort of. Routine, and the people. Though, I dunno. It matters a bit more than I let on, I think.
A: That's honest. I think that's true of a lot of us.
B: What's the singing like, then? Bet it's better than ours.
A: Well, it's loud. There's drumming. You'd —
